title: Siege in Qusra: A Toledo Man Returns to Defend His Home Against Israeli Terror
author: Michael Leonardi
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/0-2-680x499.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/21/siege-
in-qusra-a-toledo-man-returns-to-defend-his-home-against-israeli-terror/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/0-2-680x499.jpeg)

Photograph by Loai Ridi

I had already been following the siege of Qusra before Loai Ridi’s name
entered the story. Two days ago I woke up to it again in my phone’s newsfeed —
_La Repubblica_ , one of several Italian outlets that have covered the village
closely. Toledo, my hometown, was already on my mind. Lucas County -- where
Toledo is the largest city -- after more than a year of pressure from the
local Palestinian solidarity movement, had just recently decided not to renew
its five-million-dollar Israeli bond, another victory for the BDS, Boycott
Divestment and Sanctions movement.

I called a close Palestinian friend in Toledo, Afaf Adwan, originally from
Gaza. Toledo is a close-knit community. Of course she knew Loai. She put me in
contact with him. Afaf has lost many friends and family members during the
genocide in Gaza. She is on the front lines of building solidarity at home.

On the morning of August 20th I spoke with Loai from the house he is still not
allowed to leave.

Qusra is a village south of Nablus in the occupied West Bank. On or around
August 9, colonizers from nearby outposts blocked the roads, tore stones from
walls, cut the electricity and the water, and surrounded three homes belonging
to the Abu Ridi and Hassan families. They wanted the people inside to flee so
they could take the properties. Among those trapped were women and children —
nieces, nephews, relatives. Loai’s brother Qusay and his nephew were in Loai’s
house. His 83-year-old mother lives less than ten minutes away, in another
house that is also under siege. Other family members are trapped in theirs.
The entire area has been declared an off-limits military zone by the Israeli
occupation forces.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/0-1-1-680x383.jpeg)

Photograph by Loai Ridi

Loai Ridi has lived in Toledo for twenty-three years. He is a well-known
community member. He built a business of gas stations and car washes across
Northwest Ohio and Indiana. He was born and raised in Qusra. He has two
daughters. He began building a house on ancestral land in 2023 so they would
have a place in the village, a connection to their family story. For the last
eight months construction has been halted. Workers were afraid to come. Water
lines are repeatedly sabotaged. Electricity is often cut.

He watched the siege on security cameras from Toledo. After seven sleepless
nights he flew from Detroit. “I can’t let the settlers steal my house while I
was watching,” he said when he landed. He saw his mother for five minutes when
he arrived. They have not been allowed to see each other since. No one is
permitted in or out of his property.

The United Nations was allowed to deliver some food five or six days ago.
Those supplies are running out. Despite public statements from U.S. Ambassador
Mike Huckabee, the embassy in Jerusalem tells Ridi only that it is
“monitoring” the situation and trying to resolve it. There have been no other
updates. Occupation forces are parked outside the gate. Settlers roam freely
and are often seen fraternizing with the soldiers. Those soldiers are
defending the colonizers, not the families under siege.

When Loai reached the house he climbed to the roof and raised an American
flag. It did not stop a settler from walking onto his land the next morning.
He told the soldiers the man should be arrested. They told him to go back
inside.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/0-2-1-680x541.jpeg)

Photograph by Loai Ridi

From Toledo, the Jewish Community of Toledo sent him a message of solidarity.
They called the colonizers’ violence disgusting and abominable.

Huckabee, an evangelical Zionist who has long championed the colonizing of the
West Bank, called the men surrounding the houses “Israeli terrorists.” He said
their actions met the U.S. definition of terrorism: acts meant to put people
in fear for their lives and force them to change their behavior. He
distinguished them from “real settlers,” calling them “unsettlers.”

Craig Mokhiber, former director of the New York office of the UN High
Commissioner for Human Rights, rejects the language altogether:

“Palestine has already been settled for millennia, so these racist criminal
interlopers cannot rightly be called ‘settlers.’ They are not ‘settlers,’ they
are violent Zionist mobs and Israel regime paramilitaries. They do not live in
‘settlements,’ but in armed (and unlawful) colonial outposts. They are not
engaged in ‘settler clashes,’ but in lynchings and pogroms. Calling them by
their true name is important, and ending their impunity is the urgent duty of
all of humanity.”

The distinction Huckabee draws is convenient. It lets an ambassador who
supports the colonial project condemn its most visible thugs without
questioning the project itself. The outposts are illegal even under Israeli
law. The settlements they serve are illegal under international law. The army
that stands by, arrives late, prays with the attackers, and then locks the
village down is the same army that maintains the occupation and genocide. This
is not a deviation. It is a method. It is how land is taken and how a people
is made to understand that their presence is meant to be provisional.

The tactic used in Qusra — surround a home, cut it off, wait for the occupants
to break — was used last month against a family in neighboring Jalud. Rights
groups describe a coordinated strategy of displacement. The United Nations
recorded more than 2,200 Palestinians displaced by settler violence and access
restrictions in the first half of 2026 alone.

Loai Ridi’s return does not change the balance of power. It makes the theft
harder to hide. A man from Toledo flies across the world to stand on his own
roof because the alternative is to watch his family’s house disappear on a
screen. His mother is under siege a few minutes away. His brother and nephew
have already lived days without water or power. Women and children remain in
the house. The food the UN brought is running out. The embassy is
“monitoring”.

The siege of Qusra is one village in one week. It is also the logic of the
occupation, made visible because a security camera, an American passport, and
a hometown that refused to look away forced a few officials to notice.
Huckabee’s words will not end it. Neither will a flag on a roof. What remains
is that people like Loai Ridi keep returning — to a house, to a village, to
land others have decided they should not inhabit. They keep returning because
the alternative is disappearance while their continued existence becomes the
essence of resistance

This is the story from Qusra. This is the story from Toledo. It is the story
of our same common resistance.
